paragraphs: Berabbi. Chapter Ellu Terefot, 52b: “It was taught: Berabbi …” Rashi explains: “It was the name of a sage, or he was a great man and was therefore called Berabbi.” In the newer Talmud editions, in the concise rules of the Gemara: “When it mentions a sage’s name and adds the designation Berabbi—for example, Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi or Achai Berabbi—it is an expression of distinction. But when it does not mention his name and says only Berabbi—for example, ‘It was taught: Berabbi says’—then it is a proper name.” End of quotation. In Chullin 57a: “From Berabbi’s words it is apparent that he is not expert in chickens.” Rashi explains: Chizkiyah, who was a great man of his generation. There, 11b: “But was it not taught: Berabbi says?” Rashi explains: “I do not know who he is, but he is someone great in Torah, as in Eruvin 53a, Rabbi Oshaya Berabbi.” In Makkot 5b: “It was taught: Berabbi says, ‘If they have killed, they are not put to death.’ His father said”—this is also the reading in the newer Talmud editions; the reading before us is “Abaye said to him”—“‘My son, is it not an inference from the lesser to the greater …?’” Rashi explains: this was his name. In Kiddushin 21b and Bekhorot 37b: “Yudan Berabbi would expound.” Rashi explains: “His name was Yudan, and he was a great man of his generation; wherever he is called Berabbi, it expresses wisdom and acuity.” In Kiddushin 32b: “Rabbi Gamliel Berabbi stands and serves us drink.” Rashi explains: Berabbi means a great man (see Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh). Also Niddah 63b. In chapter 10 of Sanhedrin and in Chullin 137a, Rabbi said of Rabbi Yose: “Even if Berabbi’s words”—meaning Rabbi Yose’s words—“were a received tradition and the others’ words were Torah, I would take Berabbi’s words.” In Pesachim 100a, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel called Rabbi Yose “Berabbi.” Rashbam explains (see there): that is, a great man of the generation. Likewise, in Sukkah 26a, Rabbi Chiyya Berabbi; Yevamot 46, end of side b. Yuchasin writes, against the view of Dorot Olam, which said that Rabbi’s sons are called Berabbi—this is how it should read; this also caused Shalshelet HaKabbalah to err in saying that Rabbi Oshaya was Rabbi’s son; see above, Rabbi Efes—“They are Rabbi Oshaya, Rabbi Shimon, Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Chiyya Berabbi, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar Berabbi. This is a great error, for both with these and with the many others mentioned in the Talmud, as Rashi explains, it means a great man of his generation; Rabbi Oshaya is the son of Rabbi Chama bar Bisna. In the Jerusalem Talmud, what the Babylonian Talmud calls Berabbi it calls Rabbah: Rabbi Oshaya Rabbah, Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah.” End of quotation. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar Berabbi: Chullin 28a, and there, 84b, “From Berabbi’s words”; Rashi explains: an expression meaning a great man. Yevamot 105b and Kiddushin 80b: Rabbi Yochanan said, “Berabbi heard this matter”—the great man of the generation, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. In Sotah 29b, Rabbi Yochanan said, “I do not know Berabbi’s reason.” Rashi explains: the reason of Rabbi Yose, who is a sage and a great man of the generation. In Menachot 34b: Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi; Rashi explains: Yehudah the sage. Rabbi Yochanan said: “Achi Berabbi” (see his entry), Bekhorot 24b; Rashi explains: Achai Berabbi, a great and distinguished man of his generation. Rav Kohen in the name of Berabbi; Rabbi Natan Berabbi; Rami bar Berabbi; Rabbi Shimon Berabbi. See Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. In the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Peah chapter 1: “Rabbi and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi did not disagree …”; it mentions this three times in that discussion. Sedeh Yehoshua writes: “But Rabbi is Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi”—it seems to me that it should read, “But Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi is Rabbi”—“for one cannot say that this is Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, since he was not Rabbi’s disputant. It appears that the name of the disputant was omitted in print”—it had read “Rabbi So-and-so,” his name was omitted, and the word Rabbi remained—“and one should read Berabbi, with a bet, instead of Rabbi; it is the name of a sage, as Yuchasin writes.” End of quotation. This too does not seem satisfactory to me, for you will not find Berabbi as his proper name except in Chullin 11b and Makkot 5b, “It was taught: Berabbi says.” It appears that he was not a disputant of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, our holy master.
